topic: The Visual Language of Matrices: Geometric Intuition in Linear Algebra
target_audience: First-year university students or STEM-focused high school students

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Vector as a Path
sections.content: Introduce vectors not as a list of numbers, but as a movement in space starting from the origin (0,0). Establish the 'Unit Basis Vectors' (i-hat and j-hat) as the fundamental building blocks of the 2D plane.
sections.example: Pixel the Cat starts at (0,0). Moving 3 units along the x-axis and 2 units along the y-axis is represented as the vector [3, 2]. We see this as a bright arrow pointing to Pixel's new position.

sections.title: The Concept of Linear Transformation
sections.content: Define a transformation as a function that takes in one vector and spits out another. 'Linear' means the origin remains fixed and all grid lines remain parallel and evenly spaced. Use animation to show the grid warping.
sections.example: Imagine Pixel's entire world is printed on a rubber sheet. A linear transformation is like stretching or rotating that sheet without tearing it or curving the grid lines.

sections.title: The Matrix as a 'Landing Map'
sections.content: Explain that to track where *any* vector goes, we only need to track where the basis vectors (i-hat and j-hat) land. A 2x2 matrix is simply a record of these two landing spots. The first column is where i-hat landed; the second column is where j-hat landed.
sections.example: If i-hat [1, 0] lands at [1, 1] and j-hat [0, 1] lands at [-2, 0], the matrix describing this transformation is [[1, -2], [1, 0]]. We see the grid 'skew' and 'tilt' based on these new landing points.

sections.title: Visualizing Matrix-Vector Multiplication
sections.content: Show that multiplying a matrix by a vector is just a 'weighted sum' of the transformed basis vectors. It is a recipe for finding where Pixel ends up in the warped world.
sections.example: To find where Pixel [3, 2] goes, we take 3 units of the 'new' i-hat and 2 units of the 'new' j-hat. We animate the arrows chaining together to find Pixel's final transformed position.

sections.title: The Determinant: The Scaling Factor
sections.content: Introduce the determinant as the factor by which areas change during the transformation. If the determinant is 2, the area doubles. If it's 0, the world squishes into a line or a point.
sections.example: Pixel is sitting on a 1x1 square rug. After the transformation, if the rug now covers an area of 3 units, the determinant of our matrix is 3. If the rug becomes a flat line, Pixel has no room to move, and the determinant is 0.

sections.title: Summary & Intuition Check
sections.content: Recap the flow: Vectors are points -> Matrices are transformations -> Columns are basis vector destinations -> Determinants are area scales.
sections.example: Animate a quick 'gallery' of transformations: a rotation, a shear, and a flip, showing Pixel the Cat reacting to each change in his coordinate world.
